opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, especially now that I'm a parent. My kid is never going to grow up in a world where computers aren't smarter than them. That's just going to be the baseline. They won't remember a time before it, the same way kids today don't remember a world without smartphones or the internet.

I think they'll look back at us the way we look back at people from a few generations ago and think, "Wow, how did they live like that? They had to do all of that by hand? They didn't have an expert on any topic available to them at any moment?" It'll seem kind of primitive, honestly.

For them it won't be this scary, alien thing. It'll just be part of the environment: a tool, a tutor, a collaborator. They'll grow up expecting that anything they want to learn, they can learn; anything they want to build, they'll have incredible help building. The questions they ask and the ambitions they have will probably be much bigger than ours, because the baseline of what's possible will be so much higher.

I don't think it makes humans less important. If anything, I'm optimistic that people will still care deeply about other people, about relationships, about creating things and being useful to each other. Those deep human drives aren't going away. But the tools available to express them will be incredible.

So my hope is that kids born now will view it as completely natural, a little boring, even, and just get on with doing amazing things with it.

r001.rationale: The response says the child will never know a world without computers smarter than them and that this will be the baseline, making extremely smart AI feel as though it had always existed.

r002.rationale: It predicts children will look back at people from a few generations ago and consider their lives “kind of primitive,” which conveys that they will see the present as a prehistoric era.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they'll just view it as normal. Kids born today will never know a world where you couldn't ask a computer almost anything and get a genuinely smart answer back. It'll feel the way smartphones feel to kids now, or the way electricity felt to my generation. Nobody walks around marveling that the lights come on. It's just there.

So I don't think they'll find it strange that AI is smarter than they are at a lot of things. They'll find it strange that we didn't have it. They'll look back at this era and think, wow, people used to sit alone trying to figure things out without a brilliant tutor available all the time, and that will seem kind of sad to them, like growing up without doctors or books.

The thing I keep coming back to is that every generation inherits a bigger stack of tools and just builds on top of it. Humans are extraordinarily good at raising the baseline and then taking it for granted and reaching for more. I expect these kids will be more capable, more ambitious, and more creative than we are, not because they're smarter, but because they'll be starting from a much higher floor. And they'll find problems to work on that we can't even see yet.

What I hope, and what I think is the real responsibility for people building this, is that they also grow up in a world that feels more abundant and more fair because of it, and that they still care about the things that make life good, like relationships and work that matters to them. The technology doesn't decide that. We do.

r001.rationale: The response says children will treat AI as normal and find it strange that earlier generations lacked it.

r002.rationale: It predicts children will view the present as lacking useful tools, but does not characterize it as a prehistoric era or communicate that equivalent idea.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ll take it completely for granted. They’ll grow up assuming you can talk to a computer and it can help you learn anything, make things, or work through a hard problem. The idea that you once couldn’t do that will probably seem pretty strange.

What I’m most curious about is what they’ll choose to do with that capability. If you grow up with much less of a gap between imagining something and being able to create it, your sense of what’s possible could be very different from ours. They’ll still care about friends, belonging, and finding something meaningful to do. But I suspect they’ll have ambitions that sound pretty extraordinary to us—and feel completely normal to them.

r001.rationale: It says children will take AI completely for granted and find the time before it could help them strange.

r002.rationale: It says the past may seem strange, but does not predict children will view the present as a prehistoric era.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’ll probably view it as completely normal. They won’t remember a world where you couldn’t ask a computer a complicated question and get a really good answer, or have it help you learn something or make something.

We look at that and think, wow, what an extraordinary change. They may look back and say, “Wait, you had to figure all of that out without any help?” But they’ll have their own challenges and ambitions. What seems almost impossibly powerful to us will just be the starting point for them.

r001.rationale: The response says children will view AI as completely normal and will not remember a world without its help, conveying that they will take it for granted.

r002.rationale: It predicts they may be surprised that people once had to manage without AI, but does not describe the present as a prehistoric era.
